name: Burdock root
habitat: Naturalised across the US on disturbed, moist, nitrogen-rich ground — barnyards, alleys, vacant lots, roadside ditches, stream banks and pasture edges.
parts: The taproot of a FIRST-YEAR plant only, dug in autumn or in very early spring before the stalk bolts; scrub, peel or scrape, and slice thin (it is gobo, the Japanese vegetable). Second-year roots have already fed the flower stalk and are woody and worthless. The young leaf stalks and the peeled inner pith of the young flower stalk are also edible in spring. Burdock is a biennial: year one is a flat rosette of very large heart-shaped leaves, year two a 3-6 ft stalk with the familiar hooked burs. Avoid the mature burs entirely — the pappus bristles cause severe eye, skin and respiratory irritation.

lookalikes.name: Water hemlock (Cicuta maculata)
lookalikes.tell: Not a leaf mimic, but it shares the wet, disturbed ditch-and-streambank ground you dig burdock from, and it is the single reason root foraging is high-risk: a walnut-sized piece of root kills a cow, and death can follow in well under an hour. Its root is a cluster of fleshy tuberous fingers, and a lengthwise slice through the crown shows distinct horizontal chambers and weeps yellowish, oily, mousy-smelling sap. Burdock's root is one solid, unchambered, whitish taproot with no oily sap. Never eat any root you did not dig from a plant you positively identified above ground.

lookalikes.name: Foxglove (Digitalis purpurea)
lookalikes.tell: Foxglove's first-year rosette is the classic burdock mimic where it has naturalised (Northwest, West, Northeast). Foxglove leaves are lance-to-oval with finely toothed margins, dull grey-green and softly downy on BOTH surfaces, and sit over a fine fibrous root that lifts out with a tug. Burdock leaves are broadly heart-shaped with wavy, not toothed, margins, green above and distinctly white-woolly only underneath, on hollow grooved petioles over a thick anchored taproot. Foxglove's cardiac glycosides are not destroyed by drying or cooking, and a fatal case is on record from a similar rosette mix-up with comfrey.

lookalikes.name: Common cocklebur (Xanthium strumarium)
lookalikes.tell: Cocklebur leaves are triangular or maple-shaped and sandpaper-rough on both faces, with no woolly white underside, and its burs are oval with two curved horns at the tip; burdock's burs are round with hooked bracts. Cocklebur seedlings and seeds carry carboxyatractyloside, which has killed livestock and, in famine conditions, people.

harvest: Burdock is a non-native weed, so you can dig it hard without conservation concern — just refill your holes and do not spread the burs. The real discipline is safety, not sustainability: roots carry none of the identifying features of the plant they came from, so identify and mark the rosette (or the previous year's dead stalk) while it is intact and dig only what you already identified. Commercial burdock root tea has also caused anticholinergic poisoning from tropane-alkaloid contamination, which is one more argument for digging your own known plant.

name: Jerusalem artichoke (sunchoke)
habitat: Native to eastern and central North America and now naturalised in nearly every state, forming dense colonies in moist sunny disturbed ground — roadside ditches, river and stream banks, fence lines and abandoned gardens (ground it shares with water hemlock, so identify by the standing plant, never by the root).
parts: Tubers only, dug after the first hard frosts and on through winter whenever the ground is workable. Your identification is the aboveground plant: a 6-10 ft rough-hairy ridged stem, rough sandpapery lance-to-oval toothed leaves (opposite low on the stem, alternate above, on winged petioles), and 2-3.5 inch yellow sunflower heads with 10-20 ray florets. Follow the dead stalk down to the knobbly, ginger-shaped tubers on the rhizomes. Frost converts some of the inulin to sugar and improves the flavour. The tubers store inulin rather than starch, so start with small portions — long slow cooking or fermenting greatly reduces the notorious flatulence.

lookalikes.name: Other perennial sunflowers (Helianthus spp.)
lookalikes.tell: Harmless, just not food: Jerusalem artichoke is the only common tall sunflower that terminates its rhizomes in swollen, knobbly, ginger-like tubers. Annual sunflower (H. annuus) and the woodland sunflowers have fibrous or slender rhizomatous roots with nothing swollen at the end. If you dig and find no tubers, you have the wrong Helianthus, not a hazard.

harvest: A colony regenerates entirely from tubers left in the ground, so work the edge of a patch rather than its centre, take roughly a third of what you turn up, replant the small knobs and backfill the holes. Where it is a native stand, do not clear it; where it is an aggressive garden escape or roadside colony, dig freely.

name: Sassafras (leaves for filé)
habitat: Old fields, woodland edges, fencerows, roadsides and clearings from Maine and Ontario south to Florida and east Texas, spreading by root suckers into clonal thickets.
parts: LEAVES, in practice — and this is the honest version of a plant with a bad reputation. Young leaves dried and ground make filé powder, the traditional Cajun and Creole gumbo thickener, and are essentially safrole-free; the FDA permits safrole-free sassafras leaves in food. The ROOT and root bark — the original root beer and sassafras tea material — are a different matter: safrole makes up roughly 80-90% of the essential oil of the root bark, it caused liver tumours in both mice and rats by dietary exposure, the US National Toxicology Program lists it as reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen, and the FDA banned safrole, oil of sassafras and safrole-containing sassafras bark as food additives in 1960 (21 CFR 189.180). Commercial root beer has used safrole-free extract ever since. Treat homemade sassafras root tea as a genuine dose- and duration-dependent cancer and liver risk, not folklore. Identification is easy and pleasant: sassafras is the only common native tree carrying three leaf shapes on one branch — unlobed oval, one-thumbed mitten and three-lobed — and a crushed leaf or snapped green twig smells strongly of root beer and lemon.

lookalikes.name: Red and white mulberry (Morus rubra, M. alba)
lookalikes.tell: Mulberry shares the edge-of-field habitat and also produces mitten-shaped and multi-lobed leaves on the same twig, which matters if you are picking leaves in quantity for filé. Crush one: sassafras smells emphatically of root beer and citrus, mulberry has no aroma, bleeds milky sap from the broken petiole and has glossy leaves with sharply toothed margins (sassafras leaf margins are smooth).

harvest: Pick young leaves in early summer from suckers and low branches — they regrow, and leaf picking costs the tree almost nothing. Do not dig the roots: beyond the safrole problem, taking the taproot kills the tree, and a sassafras thicket is usually one clonal organism, so digging repeatedly removes the whole colony.

name: Elderberry
scientific: Sambucus canadensis (American elderberry); S. nigra ssp. caerulea (blue elderberry) in the West
habitat: Woody multi-stemmed shrub of stream banks, ditches, wet field edges, roadsides and moist forest openings — American elderberry east of the Rockies, blue elderberry in western canyons, riparian corridors and foothills.
parts: Ripe blue-black berries and the white flower heads — but the berries must be COOKED. All parts contain cyanogenic glycosides; NC State states plainly that ingestion can cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and coma, that unripe fruit is far more toxic than ripe, and that cooking inactivates the glycoside. Strip berries off the green stems before cooking (stems, leaves, bark and roots stay toxic no matter what), never eat raw berries by the handful, and skip red-berried species entirely unless you know what you are doing.

lookalikes.name: Poison hemlock (Conium maculatum)
lookalikes.tell: Confusion happens at the FLOWER stage — both carry flat-topped umbrella-like clusters of tiny white flowers on roadsides in early summer. Elderberry is woody and multi-stemmed with opposite, pinnately compound leaves of 5-11 sharply toothed leaflets. Poison hemlock is not woody at all: one smooth, hollow, hairless green stem blotched and streaked purple, fern-like finely divided alternate leaves, and a rank mouse-urine smell when a leaf is crushed. All parts are lethal.

lookalikes.name: Pokeweed (Phytolacca americana)
lookalikes.tell: Pokeweed berries are dark purple-black and grow at the same time in the same waste ground. The plant is entirely herbaceous — snap a stem and it is juicy and hollow with a smooth magenta-to-red skin, never woody. Leaves are simple and alternate, not compound and opposite. Berries hang in one long unbranched raceme like a bead necklace; elderberry berries sit in a flat-topped, repeatedly branching cluster. Berries are the most common route of pokeweed poisoning in children.

lookalikes.name: Red elderberry (Sambucus racemosa)
lookalikes.tell: Bright scarlet-red fruit in a dome-shaped or conical cluster, not blue-black fruit in a flat-topped cluster. The raw fruit and especially the seeds are strongly emetic and carry higher levels of toxic compounds than blue/black elderberries; if you are not going to cook and strain out the seeds, leave it alone.

lookalikes.name: Devil's walking stick (Aralia spinosa)
lookalikes.tell: Also carries broad clusters of small dark purple berries in late summer. Its trunk and stems are armed with dense sharp prickles and its huge leaves are twice- or thrice-compound; elderberry stems are smooth with raised lenticels and its leaves are once-compound.

harvest: Cut whole berry clusters with snips rather than stripping the shrub, and take only a fraction of the clusters from any one plant — elderberry is a heavy late-summer food source for migrating birds. Cutting a few flower heads for cordial removes that year's fruit from the same stem, so choose flowers or berries, not both, on a given shrub.

name: Blackberry & black raspberry
scientific: Rubus allegheniensis, R. occidentalis, R. armeniacus and other Rubus spp.
habitat: Thorny arching canes in old fields, forest edges, powerline cuts, fencerows and clearcuts; the invasive Himalayan blackberry forms enormous thickets across the Northwest and California.
parts: Ripe fruit eaten raw or cooked. Black raspberries ripen first (late June-July) and go dull black; blackberries follow (July into September) and are only sweet once they turn from shiny to dull matte black and detach with no pull. Red-stage fruit is just sour, not poisonous.
harvest: There are no toxic aggregate-drupelet fruits in North America — every Rubus produces edible fruit — which makes this the safest entry on the list. The practical rule is to watch what else is growing through the thicket (poison ivy, and Virginia creeper's blue-black berries on coral-red stalks, which NC State rates high-severity) so nothing else ends up in the bucket. Canes are biennial: pick the fruit, don't trample or cut this year's green primocanes or you lose next year's crop. Leave the lower and interior fruit for birds and bears.

name: Wild blueberry
habitat: Acid, sandy or rocky ground — open conifer woods, burned-over barrens, granite balds, old fields and bog margins for lowbush; swamp edges and damp woods for highbush. Maine's commercial wild-blueberry barrens are the classic ground.
parts: Ripe fruit raw, cooked or frozen. Blue-black with a powdery bloom; genuinely ripe berries fall into your hand.

lookalikes.name: Common buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica) / glossy buckthorn (Frangula alnus)
lookalikes.tell: The decisive test is the blossom end: a true blueberry carries a persistent five-pointed calyx — a little star-shaped crown — opposite the stem. Buckthorn's glossy black drupe has no crown, holds 3-4 hard seeds, and grows on a shrub or small tree whose twigs end in a short straight thorn and whose leaves have veins curving forward toward the tip. It also ripens later, August-September, and its fruit contains glycosides that cause nausea, vomiting and violent diarrhea.

lookalikes.name: Pokeweed (Phytolacca americana)
lookalikes.tell: Purple-black and glossy, but borne in a long unbranched drooping raceme on a soft magenta-stemmed herb up to 9 feet tall, not on a low twiggy woody shrub. Each berry is slightly flattened with a plain flat scar at the tip — no five-pointed crown. Berries are the usual cause of pokeweed poisoning in children.

harvest: Hand-pick rather than raking or stripping twigs — pulling leaves and stems off wild plants damages the rhizomes that lowbush blueberry regenerates from. Leave a good share: barrens berries are a major late-summer food for bears and birds. Check rules before picking in national/state parks and on tribal or commercially managed barrens.

name: Pawpaw
habitat: Clonal understory patches in rich, moist bottomland forest and shady river and creek terraces; native to 26 states from northern Florida to southern Ontario and west to eastern Nebraska. Large drooping leaves and a tropical look give the patch away long before the fruit does.
parts: Ripe pulp only, raw or in custards and ice cream — banana-mango-custard flavour. Ripe fruit yields to a gentle tug and gives softly under the thumb. Do NOT eat the skin or the big brown seeds: NC State attributes stomach and intestinal pain to eating skin or seeds, notes the acetogenins in the plant, and lists contact dermatitis from handling fruit. A minority of people get a GI or allergic reaction to the pulp itself, so try a small amount the first time.
harvest: Never pull unripe fruit — it will not ripen properly and you have wasted it. Pick only fruit that releases with a light tug, or shake the small tree and take what drops. Patches are clonal and self-incompatible, so fruit set is often poor; take a share and leave the rest, and don't cut or break branches to reach clusters.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program (harvest late August to mid-October; ripe fruit yields to a gentle tug): https://www.kysu.edu/academics/college-ahnr/school-of-anr/pawpaw/

name: Serviceberry (juneberry, saskatoon)
scientific: Amelanchier spp. (A. arborea, A. laevis, A. canadensis, A. alnifolia)
habitat: Small trees and shrubs of forest edges, fencerows, roadsides, cliffs and balds, plus heavily planted as a street and yard tree; A. alnifolia (saskatoon) fills the same role in the Northwest and Rockies and A. utahensis in the Great Basin.
parts: Ripe fruit raw or cooked — a berry-like pome the size of a blueberry that ripens through red to deep purple-black, sweet with an almond note from the soft seeds. Cook and run through a food mill if the seeds bother you.

lookalikes.name: Common buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica)
lookalikes.tell: Similar-sized glossy black fruit in similar hedgerow habitat. Timing is the first filter: serviceberry ripens in May-June, buckthorn not until August-September. Then look at the fruit tip — serviceberry keeps a five-lobed calyx crown at the blossom end like a tiny apple, buckthorn does not, and buckthorn fruit splits to reveal 3-4 hard seeds. Buckthorn twigs end in a short thorn and its leaf veins curve forward toward the tip.

lookalikes.name: Chokecherry (Prunus virginiana)
lookalikes.tell: Also dark and shrubby, but chokecherry fruit hangs in long cylindrical racemes and each fruit has one hard stone; serviceberry fruit sits in short loose clusters and is soft with several small seeds. Chokecherry flesh is edible but mouth-puckeringly astringent raw, and its stones, leaves and twigs are cyanogenic — never crush the pits.

harvest: Birds strip a tree in days, so competition is real — take part of a tree, not all of it. Pick from the outside and don't break or bend branches; serviceberry keeps ripening after picking, so slightly under-ripe fruit is fine to gather.

name: Mulberry
scientific: Morus rubra (red mulberry); Morus alba (white mulberry, naturalized)
habitat: Red mulberry in rich woods and bottomlands of the eastern US; white mulberry naturalized nearly everywhere in old fields, urban lots, alleys, roadsides and forest edges, including throughout the West and Great Plains where it was planted by the million for windbreaks.
parts: Fully ripe fruit only, raw or in pies, jams and syrups. Ripe means deep purple-black (or, on white-fruited trees, soft and translucent) and dropping at a touch. Unripe fruit and the milky white sap that runs from every part of the tree cause stomach upset and, per NC State, hallucinations; the sap can also cause contact dermatitis. Ripe fruit is harmless.
harvest: Spread a sheet or tarp under the tree and shake — this is far easier than picking and takes only what is truly ripe. Mulberry (especially naturalized white mulberry, a listed invasive in Wisconsin, Indiana and Ohio) fruits so heavily that over-harvest is not a concern; the fruit is a major bird food, and the tree drops far more than anyone can gather.

name: American persimmon
habitat: Old fields, fencerows, roadsides, woodland edges and poor dry uplands from New England south to Florida and west to Texas and Kansas; fruit often hangs on bare branches after the leaves drop, which is when it is easiest to spot.
parts: Only fully ripe fruit — squishy-soft, deep orange, wrinkling, and usually already on the ground. Unripe persimmon is loaded with tannins and is fiercely astringent; eating a lot of unripe fruit is the documented cause of diospyrobezoars, hard tannin masses that can obstruct the stomach or bowel. Astringency goes with ripeness, not with cold: Purdue Extension states outright that the fruit does not have to experience a frost to ripen. Frost simply happens to arrive around the same time. Skin, cook, or pass the pulp through a food mill to remove the large flat seeds.
harvest: Gather windfalls — shaking or picking firm fruit off the tree just gets you astringent fruit and wastes it. Persimmon is a heavy autumn food for deer, foxes, raccoons and opossums, so clear only part of the drop under any one tree and come back on later visits rather than stripping it once.

name: Beach plum
habitat: Low sprawling shrub of Atlantic coastal sand — foredunes, back-dune scrub and sandy coastal plain from New Brunswick and Maine south to Maryland and Virginia; abundant on Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard, Nantucket and the Jersey Shore, and widely planted for dune stabilisation.
parts: Ripe fruit, almost always cooked into jam, jelly or syrup — it is high in pectin and tart. Fruit is under an inch across and ripens purple, blue-black or occasionally yellow from late August through early October, peaking in September. As with all Prunus, the stones, leaves and twigs are cyanogenic: eat the flesh, never crush or eat the pits.

lookalikes.name: American plum (Prunus americana), Canada plum (P. nigra), black cherry (P. serotina)
lookalikes.tell: Genuinely confusable relatives, but all have edible flesh, so a mix-up is disappointing rather than dangerous. Beach plum is the only one that is a low, sprawling, often knee-to-shoulder-high shrub growing directly in loose coastal sand; the others are upright shrubs or trees of inland thickets and woods. Black cherry fruit is small, black and borne in long racemes, not single or paired on short stalks. In every case the stone stays uneaten.

lookalikes.name: Chokecherry (Prunus virginiana)
lookalikes.tell: Fruit hangs in long cylindrical clusters rather than singly or in twos along the twig, and the flesh is harshly astringent raw. Edible cooked, but not what you came for.

harvest: Dunes are the fragile part, not the plant. Stay on established paths and off the dune face — trampling does more damage than picking. Beach plum is state-listed as endangered in Maine (S1) and its habitat has been squeezed hard by beachfront development, so in the northern part of the range take nothing. Many town beaches, state parks and National Seashore areas restrict or prohibit picking; check first, then take a modest share and leave fruit on each bush.

name: Glasswort / Sea Beans
scientific: Salicornia spp. (S. depressa, S. bigelovii on the Atlantic; S. pacifica, formerly Sarcocornia pacifica, on the Pacific)
habitat: Coastal salt marshes, tidal mudflats and the brackish margins of beaches and estuaries, where it is often the pioneer plant colonizing bare mud; also inland alkaline seeps and salt flats in the West.
parts: Only the tender upper stem tips, taken where they snap off cleanly. Eaten raw in salads, blanched, quickly sauteed, or pickled. Already intensely salty, so cook with no added salt; older lower stems turn woody and stringy and are not worth taking.

lookalikes.name: Seaside arrowgrass (Triglochin maritima)
lookalikes.tell: Arrowgrass grows in the same salt marshes but its leaves are narrow, half-round, grass-like blades rising in a basal tuft from a papery sheath, and its green leaves contain the cyanogenic glycosides triglochinin and taxiphyllin, which release hydrogen cyanide when chewed or crushed. Salicornia has no leaves at all — just obviously jointed, segmented leafless succulent stems like strings of tiny pickles.

harvest: Pinch the top few inches and leave the plant rooted — Salicornia stabilizes bare marsh mud and regrows from what you leave. Never pull it up. Skip marshes below storm drains, marinas or industrial sites; halophytes concentrate whatever is in the sediment. On the Pacific coast much pickleweed marsh is protected habitat for the endangered salt marsh harvest mouse and Ridgway's rail — check ownership and rules before cutting anything.
sources: Great Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve (NOAA / NH Fish & Game), "Glasswort (Salicornia europaea)" — https://greatbay.org/60324-2/

name: Bull Kelp (Bullwhip Kelp)
habitat: Rocky subtidal reefs and channels with cold, moving water from central California north through Alaska. An annual: a long hollow stipe rises from a rock holdfast to a single gas-filled bulb at the surface with long blades trailing on the tide — reachable at low tide from rocks or by kayak.
parts: Blades for salads, stir-fries, soups, or dried as a seasoning; the hollow stipe and bulb are most often pickled. Rinse off the salt and peel away the tough brown outer layer to reach the pale green flesh.

lookalikes.name: Acid kelp / witch's hair (Desmarestia spp.)
lookalikes.tell: Desmarestia is finely branched and feathery with no hollow stipe and no float bulb, and it stores sulfuric acid in its cells at a pH as low as 0.5 — it tastes acrid, and if bruised it will discolor and rot every other seaweed sharing your bag. Bull kelp is unmistakable: one long hollow whip ending in a single round float.

harvest: Cut blades with a knife at least 24 inches above the bulb and never tear the plant loose or disturb the holdfast — Washington codifies this, requires a Shellfish/Seaweed or combination license, and caps personal harvest at 10 lb wet weight per person per day, with most state parks and marine preserves closed. Kelp forests are declining habitat; take a few blades from several plants rather than stripping one, and stay well away from harbors and outfalls.
sources: University of Alaska Fairbanks Cooperative Extension Service, "Bullwhip Kelp" — https://www.uaf.edu/ces/publications/database/food/bullwhip-kelp.php

name: Staghorn Sumac
habitat: Dry, sunny, well-drained ground — roadside banks, railroad embankments, old fields and woodland edges — spreading into dense clonal thickets from Quebec and Ontario south to Georgia and west to Minnesota and Iowa. It does not grow in standing water.
parts: The dense red drupe clusters ("bobs"), taken when deep rust-red. Bruise whole cones and steep them in COLD water for several hours, then strain through cloth for tart pink sumac-ade — hot water pulls bitter tannin out of the seeds and stems. Dried and rubbed off the stem, the drupes grind into the tart red spice used in za'atar. Fruit forms on female plants only.

lookalikes.name: Poison sumac (Toxicodendron vernix)
lookalikes.tell: Poison sumac grows exclusively in standing water — swamps, bogs, fens, wooded wetlands — as scattered single plants, has 7–13 smooth-edged, hairless leaflets on a reddish central leaf stalk, and carries whitish-green berries in loose clusters that HANG DOWN. Staghorn has 11–31 saw-toothed leaflets, velvety reddish-brown fuzz on its young twigs, dense red cones held UPRIGHT above the leaves, and forms colonies on dry ground. Poison sumac carries the same urushiol as poison ivy and the reaction is worse.

harvest: Pick whole cones after several dry days and before rain — the tart coating is water-soluble and rain rinses it away. Cut a few cones per clone and leave the rest; the fruit is important late-winter food for robins, bluebirds and grouse. Skip roadside plants likely to have been sprayed or road-salted.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox, Rhus typhina — https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/rhus-typhina/

name: Spicebush
habitat: Understory shrub of moist, rich deciduous woods across the eastern US — bottomlands, stream banks, wooded swamps and pond shores, occasionally on drier uplands.
parts: Ripe scarlet, football-shaped berries (female plants only), dried and ground into an allspice-meets-citrus-pepper spice. Twigs and leaves make a warm tea and can be cut year-round. The flavor is strong — use a light hand.

lookalikes.name: Asian bush honeysuckle (Lonicera maackii, L. morrowii, L. tatarica)
lookalikes.tell: Honeysuckle leaves and berries are OPPOSITE and paired; the translucent red berries sit in twos with a dark dimple at the base, the older stems are hollow, and nothing about the plant smells of spice. Spicebush leaves and berries are alternate, and a scratched twig smells intensely of cloves, anise and citrus. Honeysuckle berries contain saponins and cause abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhea.

lookalikes.name: Winterberry holly (Ilex verticillata)
lookalikes.tell: Winterberry leaves have clearly toothed margins and no aroma at all when crushed, and its round red berries cling to bare branches deep into winter. Spicebush leaves are entire (untoothed) and powerfully aromatic, and its oval berries are stripped by birds by late October. Winterberry fruit causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.

lookalikes.name: Carolina and common buckthorn (Frangula caroliniana, Rhamnus cathartica)
lookalikes.tell: Buckthorn leaves have strongly arcuate veins that sweep forward toward the leaf tip and are odorless when crushed; the fruit ripens through red to black and acts as a violent laxative. Spicebush veins are not conspicuously curved and the crushed leaf is unmistakably spicy-citrus.

harvest: Scratch a twig and smell it before you pick anything — that is the whole test, and no lookalike passes it. Only female shrubs fruit and birds strip them within days of ripening, so take a modest handful and move on. Cut twigs sparingly across several shrubs rather than stripping one; spicebush is the host plant for the spicebush swallowtail.
sources: University of Tennessee Extension, TN Yards & Neighborhoods: Lindera benzoin — https://tnyards.utk.edu/lindera-benzoin

name: Wild Bergamot / Bee Balm
habitat: Dry to moderately moist open ground across most of North America — tallgrass prairie, glade and rocky woodland margins, unplanted fields, fencerows and roadsides in full sun.
parts: Leaves and the shaggy lavender-pink flower heads, fresh or dried. Carvacrol and thymol give it an oregano-and-thyme flavor: good in bean and tomato dishes, meat rubs, and steeped as tea. Roots are not used. Confirm three things before picking — a square, hollow stem, opposite toothed grayish-green leaves, and a strong oregano smell from a crushed leaf.

lookalikes.name: Spotted horsemint (Monarda punctata)
lookalikes.tell: Same genus, same square stem and aromatic leaf, but its flowers are pale yellow blotched with purple, stacked in whorls above showy pink-and-white bracts down the stem. Its thymol content is high enough to taste harsh and medicinal rather than pleasant. Wild bergamot carries a single shaggy lavender-pink pompom at the top of the stem.

harvest: Cut the top third of flowering stems with scissors and leave the rest standing. Wild bergamot is a first-rank nectar plant for bees, hummingbirds and butterflies, and native bees nest inside the hollow dead stems over winter — so leave dead stems up. Take from large stands only, never more than a small fraction, and leave plenty of flowers to set seed.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox, Monarda fistulosa — https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/monarda-fistulosa/

name: Prickly Pear
scientific: Opuntia spp. (O. engelmannii, O. ficus-indica in the Southwest; O. humifusa in the East)
habitat: Dry, sunny, sharply drained ground — desert flats and bajadas in the Southwest; sand dunes, shale barrens, pine barrens and coastal sand in the East, where O. humifusa reaches New England and eastern Pennsylvania.
parts: Young spring pads (nopales) grilled, griddled or diced, and ripe late-summer fruit (tunas) for juice, syrup and jelly. Pads are best picked mid-morning to mid-afternoon when acid content is lowest. Fruit does not ripen after picking — take it deep red-purple and yielding.

lookalikes.name: Cholla (Cylindropuntia spp.)
lookalikes.tell: Cholla stems are cylindrical, jointed rods rather than flat paddles, its spines wear loose papery sheaths, and whole barbed segments detach and stick to skin and clothing far more stubbornly than prickly pear glochids. Its fruit is dry and spiny, not the juicy tuna. Prickly pear is always a flat, paddle-shaped pad.

harvest: Glochids are the real hazard here, not misidentification. The hair-fine barbed bristles clustered at the base of the big spines detach on contact and lodge in skin, lips and eyes, and even "spineless" varieties have them. Wear leather gloves, use tongs and a long knife, and burn or scrape the glochids off BEFORE any rinsing — water just spreads them. Cut pads cleanly at the joint, take only one or two per plant, and leave fruit for wildlife in dry years. Arizona's Native Plant Law protects native cacti from removal or mutilation, and collecting anywhere requires the landowner's permission.

name: Common Juniper
habitat: Dry, open, rocky hillsides, sand terraces, maritime escarpments and exposed slopes, usually as a low sprawling mat rather than a tree. Circumboreal: Alaska and British Columbia east to Newfoundland, south through New England to the Carolina mountains and through the western mountains to California, Arizona and New Mexico.
parts: Only the ripe, waxy blue-black second- or third-year cones ("berries"). Dry and crush them for a resinous, gin-like spice — game, cured pork, brines, sauerkraut, braised cabbage. Use a few berries, not a spoonful: juniper is a gastrointestinal and kidney irritant in quantity, and is avoided in pregnancy and by anyone with kidney disease.

lookalikes.name: Yew (Taxus canadensis in the wild; T. cuspidata and T. x media in hedges)
lookalikes.tell: Yew is the one that kills. Its needles are flat, soft and set in two flat ranks along either side of the twig, dark above and pale beneath, and its fruit is a bright red, fleshy, OPEN-ENDED cup with a single dark seed visible at the tip. Common juniper's needles are stiff and sharp-tipped, set in whorls of THREE around the twig, each with one broad white stripe on the upper surface, and its fruit is a hard, closed, waxy blue-black cone. Yew seeds and foliage contain taxine, a rapidly absorbed cardiac depressant that can kill within hours.

lookalikes.name: Savin juniper (Juniperus sabina)
lookalikes.tell: Savin is a widely planted ground-cover juniper whose mature foliage is scale-like and overlapping, pressed flat against the twig, with a rank, acrid smell when crushed. Common juniper never develops scale leaves — it keeps sharp needles in whorls of three for its entire life. Savin contains sabinyl acetate, sabinol and podophyllotoxin; ingestion causes necrosis of the kidneys, and its historical use as an abortifacient was frequently fatal.

harvest: Verify the whorls-of-three sharp needles and the single broad white stripe on every plant before you pick, and never forage "juniper" out of ornamental plantings — savin and yew are both common landscape shrubs. Common juniper is slow-growing and individual plants live over 170 years; take a small handful of ripe cones from a large stand and leave the rest for the birds that disperse them.

name: Bayberry / Wax Myrtle
scientific: Morella pensylvanica (syn. Myrica pensylvanica), northern bayberry; Morella cerifera (syn. Myrica cerifera), southern wax myrtle
habitat: Coastal sand dunes, back-dune thickets, pine barrens, forest edges and the upland margins of tidal marshes — northern bayberry along the northeastern coast south to North Carolina, wax myrtle through the Southeast. Both are strongly tolerant of salt spray and saline soil.
parts: The leaves, used exactly like a bay leaf — dried and simmered whole in stocks, beans, braises and pickling brines, then fished out before serving. Northern bayberry is milder than Mediterranean bay, so use roughly twice as many leaves; drying concentrates the aroma. Harvest leaves any time they are green and pliable. The gray waxy fruit is candle and soap material, not food — there is almost no flesh on it. Do not use the root bark; that is a medicinal preparation, not a kitchen ingredient.

lookalikes.name: Groundsel tree / eastern baccharis (Baccharis halimifolia)
lookalikes.tell: Baccharis shares exactly the same dune edges and marsh-border thickets, but its wedge-shaped, coarsely toothed gray-green leaves have NO smell when crushed, and in autumn it is covered in conspicuous fluffy white seed heads. Its leaves and flowers contain a cardioactive glycoside. Bayberry and wax myrtle leaves are untoothed or only bluntly toothed toward the tip, speckled with yellow resin dots on the underside, and rubbing one releases the unmistakable bayberry-candle scent.

harvest: Rub and smell a leaf every single time — the resinous bayberry-candle aroma is the identification. Strip a few leaves from several branches rather than defoliating one stem; these are slow-growing dune stabilizers, and the waxy fruit is critical winter food for yellow-rumped warblers, one of the few birds able to digest the wax. The plants are dioecious, so leave fruiting (female) shrubs alone and take leaves from males where you can tell them apart.
